En entrant dans la salle funéraire, on p: Walking into the funeral home, you could immediately see, around the casket, the many bouquets of flowers that the Ahuntsic community had left in front of Mr. Yong’s store. He was killed in his convenience store on November 6. The gesture is a fitting expression of the love, sadness and deep solidarity that has surrounded his family since the fatal attack at Dépanneur de Lille in Ahuntsic.
Selon Danny Morin, qui travaille au comm: According to Danny Morin, who works at the neighbouring business and witnessed the tragedy, three young men in their early twenties walked into the convenience store at lunchtime with a knife and took the owner’s life. After committing this irreparable act in broad daylight, they walked out casually with a case of beer. The culprits have still not been found. Mr. Yong’s family members fear so much for their safety that they did not want his full name made public, a request we agreed to out of respect.
Quand elle a eu vent du drame, Julie Gou: When she heard about the tragedy, Julie Gougeon, a regular customer, did not want the family to feel alone in this ordeal and wanted them to know the community stood behind them. The day after the murder, she organized a vigil in front of the store, where more than fifty people came to pay tribute to the owner. They left many cards, letters and bouquets of flowers, which are now gathered around the casket.

« On n’avait personne quand on a immigré: “We had no one when we immigrated here to Canada from China,” said a friend of the family who was at the funeral and preferred to remain anonymous, speaking to us in Mandarin. “Mr. Yong’s family and mine, we shared the same culture, so we helped each other and looked after one another in this foreign country.” That is how a strong friendship was born, one that has lasted more than thirty years. Over many years of support and solidarity, the two families grew close and consider one another members of the same family.
Le départ inattendu de M. Yong, un père: The unexpected loss of Mr. Yong, a 49-year-old father, has been very hard on everyone. It is obvious that family values were very important to this convenience store owner. His loved ones put together a long slideshow filled with photos of wonderful memories: Mr. Yong on a bike with his son behind him, all smiles; Mr. Yong on a snowy outing pulling his children on a sled; Mr. Yong celebrating several birthdays in front of big cakes with his loved ones.
« C’est comme ça que je me rappelle de M: “That’s how I remember Mr. Yong,” says Ms. Gougeon as she watches the slideshow. She and her partner had been going to the store for several years to do their regular shopping, preferring to support their little corner convenience store over the big supermarket chains. “He was a very generous man who knew his customers and took care of them. Mr. Yong even told my partner he smoked too much!” she recalls. Ms. Gougeon is not the only one who holds a warm memory of the owner.
Camille Duchesne, une autre cliente régu: Camille Duchesne, another regular customer, preferred Mr. Yong’s store to others closer to her home for the same reasons. “I liked going to him precisely because he was the owner. He was really friendlier than the others,” she explains to me, describing an always cheerful man whom she visited every day for her daily cigarettes. “He [recognized] everybody’s orders. When I changed my order a little, he always noticed.”
Quand elle a entendu la nouvelle, Mme Du: When she heard the news, Ms. Duchesne initially couldn’t believe it. “I remember crying, not necessarily from sadness, but really from anger,” she recalls. When she finally realized it was indeed her favourite convenience store, her rage led her to create <l1>a fundraising campaign</l1> with her boyfriend to help the family through this ordeal. The campaign was shared with her loved ones and several Facebook groups in the Ahuntsic neighbourhood. Calvin Wu, Mr. Yong’s cousin, heard about the campaign and kept sharing it with his circle, where it was a great success. In less than two weeks, more than $13,000 was raised.
« C’est des choses qui arrivent », dit-i: “These things happen,” he says. “It could happen to anyone on the street. We just didn’t expect it to happen to us. But well, we have to do everything we can now to get through it.”
Il a aussi commencé sa propre <l1>campag: He has also started his own <l1>fundraising campaign</l1> to support the widow, since she will no longer be able to work after this tragedy and has three children to support. Mr. Wu was determined to honour his cousin, who had dedicated his life to supporting his family, and to help them cover school fees for the children who are still minors. At the time of publication of this article, the campaign had raised more than $5,000.
« On est là pour être solidaire avec eux: “We’re here to stand in solidarity with them. He’s one of us, a small shopkeeper from the Chinese diaspora like us,” says a woman who preferred to remain anonymous, speaking in Mandarin. “When something like this happens, we really have to make noise so people understand that it’s unacceptable and that we won’t just take it.” Like more than thirty people at the funeral, this woman did not know Mr. Yong personally, but she shared his trade.
Ce groupe d’étrangers, unis par une même: This group of strangers, united by the same culture and the same profession and coming from all over the Montréal area, had gathered in a lounge. The shopkeepers shared their common stories, their outrage over this act against one of their own, and their calls to action. Most are immigrants of Chinese origin in their fifties who arrived in Quebec in the 1990s, as Mr. Yong had. In this group, sadness turned into anger that pushed them to act. No one wanted Mr. Yong to be forgotten. They wanted to do everything they could to honour the dignity of his life and make sure his death was not in vain.
En effet, lorsqu’on les laisse s’exprime: Indeed, when they are allowed to express themselves in their mother tongue, it is extremely clear that all the Chinese shopkeepers present want to be heard. “I don’t understand why it’s not being talked about in the newspapers,” another shopkeeper, the owner of a tobacco shop in Laval, told me in Mandarin. “In the early 1990s, my sister was attacked in her store. It made the front page of the Journal de Montréal. I’m in shock that this event isn’t making the front page of the major papers.”
Tout comme les deux autres femmes qui ét: Like the two other women sitting beside her, she has genuinely feared for her safety at work since that sordid event. Moreover, many shopkeepers at the funeral expressed a feeling of insecurity about their trade because of the pandemic and the regular vandalism they face.
« On doit être solidaires avec les autre: “We have to stand in solidarity with other small shopkeepers, no matter where they come from, because we all have the same problems,” says Wuhen Taxue, a small shopkeeper whose neighbouring store had its windows smashed last week. Other shopkeepers also have no shortage of stories about theft, vandalism and customers who harass them. Shuling Chen, a former small shopkeeper, is fed up with people in power ignoring these problems and the shopkeepers’ demands. In a passionate speech that the group of Chinese shopkeepers listened to attentively, he called for mobilization.
“One person can convince three. If we mobilize the whole Chinese community around this, we’ll be heard. We’ll say that we’re angry and that we’re sad, loud and clear,” he declares in Mandarin. “We have to keep taking action nonstop and act to put pressure on people!” Zi Xiang, another former small shopkeeper, followed with his own speech in Mandarin, in which he proposed concrete actions. “We’re going to organize a full day of demonstrations in the streets downtown, and we’re going to write open letters to politicians and to police stations,” he declares.
« On va avoir des pancartes dans les vit: “We’re going to put signs in the windows of our convenience stores to protest this. If one person does something, the others will follow. We, the Chinese diaspora, really have to make ourselves heard when things like this happen!” At this announcement, the entire crowd applauded.
Bei Shan, une journaliste de Shanghai ét: Bei Shan, a journalist from Shanghai who has lived in Montréal since 2015, was also at the funeral. She believes the community’s silence is due to several factors: “There are a lot more convenience stores than people think, but we just forget about them because the Chinese owners don’t speak the language.”
Selon elle, la barrière de la langue et: According to her, the language barrier and Asian people’s sense of insecurity in Montréal silence their many demands. “Immigrants, far from where they were born, choose to be quiet and hard-working,” says the host of the show Montrenese, sharply criticizing the model minority myth. “I know they need someone who wants to […] step out and speak up [for the community].” Moreover, Marvin Rotrand, city councillor for Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, a borough with a large Asian population, passed <l1>a motion denouncing hate acts against people of Asian origin</l1> last June.
La motion, appuyée par plusieurs organis: The motion, backed by several Asian organizations, the Concordia Student Union, the McGill University student association, and the Centre de Recherche-Action sur les Relations Raciales (CRARR), is a historic step toward denouncing the rise of anti-Asian racism. Among other things, the motion asks city council to ensure the safety of Montrealers of Asian origin.
Mais entre-temps, la communauté est déjà: But in the meantime, the community is already taking matters into its own hands. Jimmy Chan and Eddy Li, an activist for the Asian community and the owner of a security guard company, have worked together to create a professional security unit that will patrol Chinatown every night. SPVM Unit 21 met with them to collaborate on neighbourhood safety, a spirit of cooperation that is very unusual for police officers.
Le meurtre de M. Yong est-il un crime ha: Was Mr. Yong’s murder a hate crime? It is hard to know at this stage, but the CRARR reports a rise in hate crime cases against Asian people since the start of the year. The organization offers pro bono legal aid services to victims of hate crimes, who are often left to fend for themselves and lack information on how to proceed. The organization currently offers services in Mandarin and Cantonese, in addition to French and English. Mr. Niemi advises victims to <l1>contact his organization</l1> as soon as possible after an attack so that they are informed of their options and avoid mistakes made out of ignorance.
Bien loin du stéréotype de la minorité m: Far from the stereotype of the silent model minority so often attributed to them, it is clear that Asian people thirst for change. They are ready to organize to stand in solidarity with one of their own who left too soon, to defend their interests and to defend their place in Quebec.
